extracted.intended_audience: law and economics scholars, patent policymakers, and economists studying patent policy
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluate the economic and institutional functions of the patent system (reward vs prospect functions) and policy reforms (compulsory licensing, disclosure rules, government patent policy, trade secrets, subsidies, research organization). Focus is on how rules affect incentives, coordination, transaction costs, and technological development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market share and unified patents reduce competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the market share of the unified patents is significant, they have tended to see a loss of competition in an important factor of production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A high market share held via unified patent ownership can reduce competition in key productive inputs; patent policy should be attentive to market-concentration effects of unified patent portfolios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prospect function complicates ownership fragmentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The prospects generated by the patent system are largely shaped by technological history. Ownership of different parts of what can be most efficiently exploited as one prospect may be in different hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because efficient exploitation of a technological prospect may require unified control of multiple patents, policy should permit or facilitate rearrangement of control among patent owners to realize efficiency gains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for mechanisms to permit unification of control when efficient
rubrics_metrics.description: The only way to obtain the efficiency gains of a prospect may be to permit the parties to rearrange control of the various patents involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous to mineral claims where later development shows unified control is optimal (single shaft, safety), patent institutions should allow unification (through licensing, pooling, mergers, etc.) where it improves exploitation efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdependence of closely related patents creates risk of blocking
rubrics_metrics.description: Two patents may be so closely related that it makes sense to look for improvements to both at once, or, conversely, the search for improvements to one may carry the risk that that improvement will infringe the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent holders and policy should recognize that fragmented ownership of interrelated claims can deter or distort R&D because innovators avoid work that risks infringing other patents; coordination mechanisms (cross-licenses, pools) mitigate this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fragmented ownership distorts firms' research strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: If ownership of the patents was not unified, then each firm would have to shape its research program in relation to its patent position although that might not be the most efficient research strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical and legal attention should be paid to industries (e.g., 'cracking patents') where dispersed ownership forces firms to limit research to avoid infringement rather than pursue socially optimal improvements; the law should facilitate technical interchange where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreements should address efficient management and coordination
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of agreements of this type should be examined to determine how they address the problem of efficient management and coordination of effort by the firms to increase the value of the patents involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or drafting industry agreements, analyze how they allocate rights, permit cooperation, and manage joint development to raise patent value without unduly harming competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open availability/pooling as a simple coordination solution
rubrics_metrics.description: One simple solution may be to simply make all patents available to all firms with an important position and let everyone begin again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent pools or broad availability can eliminate blocking and re-start innovation, but tradeoffs with incentives and returns to inventors must be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compulsory licensing destroys the prospect function
rubrics_metrics.description: Any form of compulsory licensing destroys the prospect function because the patent owner loses the ability to control who can use the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under compulsory licensing third parties can search for ways to increase the value of the patent and, when they find it, force the owner to license at a regulated rate. Policymakers should weigh this loss of owner control against desired output/competition benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government patent policy: free use vs exclusive licenses tradeoff
rubrics_metrics.description: The reward function suggests free use of inventions (viewed as already made). The prospect function suggests the granting of exclusive licenses of patents (viewed as in need of further development).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Government decisions whether to make patents freely available or to grant exclusive licenses should balance the immediate reward/disclosure benefits against the need to preserve incentives for further development (prospect realization).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure must be sufficient and timely to enable others to use invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The reward theory has tended to emphasize the disclosure role of the patent. In exchange for his invention, the inventor gets a seventeen-year monopoly. But this is only so if the disclosure of the invention in the patent is sufficient to enable others to use it; otherwise the inventor may have both the patent and secrecy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because patent applications may be filed years before commercialization, statutory disclosure requirements risk failing to provide economically meaningful information at the time of market use; assess both sufficiency and timing of disclosure rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent description's practical purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose of the description in the patent is not to disclose the commercially relevant technology, but to provide a context in which the legal limits of the claim acquire meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory efforts should recognize that formal patent text serves legal delimitation more than tech transfer; forcing longer formal disclosures may not increase practical dissemination of know-how.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid raising disclosure costs without increasing meaningful information
rubrics_metrics.description: Efforts ... to increase the amount of disclosure in patent documents in pursuit of the ideal of the reward theory ... raise the cost and complexity of patents without increasing the amount of economically meaningful information disseminated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative or procedural changes aimed solely at more detailed formal disclosures should be scrutinized for actual economic benefit versus administrative cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade secrecy complements patents and reduces patent system cost
rubrics_metrics.description: Trade secrecy, operating in the context of a patent system, reduces the cost of the patent system. If patents cover the basic framework of the technology, then less important but nevertheless costly and valuable information can be protected by trade secrets but exchanged and disclosed within the protective framework of the patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing coexistence of patents (for core frameworks) and trade secrets (for peripheral but valuable details) can reduce the incentive to over-patent and lower system costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secrecy can improve enforceability of process patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules that permit the patentee to retain important information makes patents that can be infringed in secrecy more enforceable. Process patents can be infringed without alerting the patent owner to that fact. But if potential infringers must obtain information from the patent owner before they infringe, their ability to infringe without notice to the owner is greatly reduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider procedural and contractual arrangements that require contact with patentee to obtain necessary know-how, thereby making covert infringement less likely and enforcement more practical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government subsidy risks reducing technological improvement if it replaces patent property
rubrics_metrics.description: Government subsidy of applied research has been seen as a way to create incentives for research while avoiding the output constraint of a patent. But if government subsidy brings with it a loss of the patent property system, it may have the effect of reducing rather than increasing the rate of technological improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subsidy programs should be designed so that patent rights (or equivalent private incentives) are preserved or managed efficiently (e.g., allow private subsidized firms to identify and keep patents) to avoid displacement of private R&D.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent system cannot perform prospect function for basic research
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent system cannot perform the prospect function in the context of basic research because of the inability to fashion a meaningful property right around an explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternative institutional mechanisms (peer review, publication customs, exclusive rights for first proposers, etc.) need to be evaluated for their ability to coordinate basic-research searchers and disseminate early information; examine whether decision power must rest with peers and the limits on any exclusivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal-culture evidence: property rights lower transaction costs and interferences signal duplicative search
rubrics_metrics.description: The legal culture provides two kinds of data useful to the task. First, it shows how defined property rights in information significantly lower the costs of transactions concerning such information. And second, the frequency of interferences within the patent system indicates that the problem of duplicative search is not a negligible one in the development of technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing patent-system effects, use metrics such as transaction-cost reduction from well-defined rights and the rate of patent interferences as indicators of duplicative search and coordination failure.
